title: Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, 471 Penal Code: Bail & Defense in Bangladesh
metaDescription: Are Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, and 471 Penal Code bailable in Bangladesh? Learn bail procedures, forgery penalties, and High Court Section 561A defense.
heroIntro: In Bangladesh, financial disagreements, failed commercial partnerships, and disputed land transactions are frequently converted into aggressive criminal cases by invoking Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the Penal Code 1860. Complainants bundle allegations of criminal breach of trust, cheating, and document forgery to secure police arrest or exert overwhelming settlement leverage. For business owners, property holders, and non-resident Bangladeshis implicated in such cases, understanding which sections are bailable, how bail is secured under the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC), and how the High Court Division quashes frivolous proceedings under Section 561A CrPC is critical to safeguarding personal liberty.

quickAnswer.title: Are Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, and 471 Penal Code Bailable in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Under Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898, Section 420 (cheating) is technically bailable as a standalone offence, whereas Section 406 (criminal breach of trust), Section 467 (forgery of valuable security), and Section 468 (forgery for cheating) are non-bailable offences. Section 471 (using a forged document) takes the bailable or non-bailable status of the underlying forged instrument. When these sections are combined in an FIR or complaint, the entire case is treated as non-bailable by the police and Magistrate, requiring formal bail applications under Section 497 CrPC or anticipatory bail before the High Court Division under Section 498 CrPC.
highlights: Section 420 is bailable, but Section 406 and Section 467 are strictly non-bailable.
Combining non-bailable sections removes police station bail entitlement.
Section 467 carries potential life imprisonment or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years.
Civil disputes disguised as criminal cases can be quashed under Section 561A CrPC.

Key Defense Mechanism: Distinguishing civil breach of contract from dishonest fraudulent inducement.

sections.title: 1. Statutory Breakdown: What Each Section Penalizes
sections.content:
The Penal Code 1860 contains an extensive framework criminalizing financial deception, breach of fiduciary obligations, and documentary falsification. To evaluate legal exposure, an accused individual must understand the distinct statutory ingredients of each frequently cited section:

  • Section 406 (Criminal Breach of Trust): Punishes anyone who dishonestly misappropriates, converts to their own use, or disposes of property entrusted to them in violation of any legal direction or contractual duty. Penalty: imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both.
  • Section 420 (Cheating and Dishonestly Inducing Delivery of Property): Requires proof that the accused cheated the victim and dishonestly induced them to deliver any property, or make, alter, or destroy the whole or part of a valuable security. Penalty: imprisonment up to 7 years and mandatory fine.
  • Section 467 (Forgery of Valuable Security, Will, etc.): Criminalizes the forgery of documents purporting to be a valuable security, a will, or an authority to adopt or receive money. Penalty: imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment up to 10 years, and fine.
  • Section 468 (Forgery for Purpose of Cheating): Punishes the act of committing forgery intending that the document shall be used for cheating. Penalty: imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.
  • Section 471 (Using as Genuine a Forged Document): Imposes criminal liability on anyone who fraudulently or dishonestly uses as genuine any document which they know or have reason to believe to be a forged document. The punishment mirrors the penalty for the actual forgery.

sections.title: 2. Bailable vs. Non-Bailable Classifications under Schedule II CrPC
sections.content:
A widespread misconception among defendants in Bangladesh is that because Section 420 is the primary charge, bail can be claimed as a matter of right at the police station or before the Magistrate. The legal reality is determined strictly by the classification table in Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898.

Under Schedule II, Section 420 is categorized as a cognizable and bailable offence. In contrast, Section 406 is cognizable and non-bailable. Furthermore, Section 467 and Section 468 are both classified as cognizable, non-bailable, and non-compoundable offences. For Section 471, the bail status corresponds directly to whether the underlying document forged was bailable or non-bailable.

When an FIR (First Information Report) or a Complaint Register (CR) case includes both bailable and non-bailable sections, the entire case is governed by non-bailable procedural rules. Police officers cannot release the suspect on personal bond, and the court must evaluate any release application under the judicial discretion governed by Section 497 of the CrPC.

sections.title: 3. Strategic Bundling: Why Complainants Combine Sections 406, 420 & 467
sections.content:
In day-to-day legal practice across Dhaka and the district courts, complainants routinely combine Sections 406 and 420 alongside forgery sections. In strict legal theory, Section 406 and Section 420 are antithetical: Section 406 presupposes lawful entrustment of property followed by dishonest conversion, whereas Section 420 requires dishonest intention from the very inception of the transaction that induced the victim to part with property.

Despite this mutual exclusivity, complainants routinely draft omnibus complaints alleging both entrustment and initial fraudulent deception, then add Section 467 by claiming that a receipt, deed, cheque, or power of attorney was fabricated. The strategic objective is twofold: first, to ensure the offences are non-bailable so that the accused faces immediate arrest; second, to elevate the potential sentence to life imprisonment under Section 467, thereby preventing summary disposal and increasing settlement pressure.

Courts are well aware of this tendency. When assessing bail, experienced judges scrutinize the complaint to determine whether the inclusion of Section 467 is supported by concrete documentary evidence or is merely a colorable device engineered to prevent bail on a commercial transaction.

sections.title: 4. Regular Bail Procedure in the Magistrate and Sessions Courts
sections.content:
If an accused person is arrested by law enforcement or voluntarily surrenders before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (CMM) or Chief Judicial Magistrate (CJM), the defense must file an application for regular bail under Section 497 of the CrPC.

Under Section 497(1), bail shall not be granted if there appear reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has been guilty of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life. Because Section 467 carries potential life imprisonment, Magistrate Courts frequently decline bail on jurisdictional caution, particularly during the early stages of police investigation before the filing of a formal Police Report (Charge Sheet) under Section 173 CrPC.

However, the proviso to Section 497(1) grants the court discretion to release any person who is under sixteen years of age, a woman, or sick or infirm. Furthermore, under Section 497(2), if the court satisfies itself that there are no reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed a non-bailable offence, but that there are sufficient grounds for further inquiry, the accused shall be released on bail pending such inquiry. If the Magistrate rejects bail, the defense immediately moves a bail petition before the Sessions Judge or Metropolitan Sessions Judge under Section 498 CrPC. For a broader overview of regular surrender, review our guide on regular bail under Section 497 CrPC.

sections.title: 5. Anticipatory Bail Before the High Court Division (Section 498 CrPC)
sections.content:
When an individual discovers that an FIR has been lodged at a police station or a warrant of arrest has been issued in a CR case under Sections 406, 420, and 467, remaining at liberty is critical to mounting an effective defense. Under Section 498 of the CrPC, the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh possesses concurrent jurisdiction to grant anticipatory bail (pre-arrest bail).

Anticipatory bail is an extraordinary equitable remedy. The Supreme Court Appellate Division in landmark rulings has established that to obtain anticipatory bail, the applicant must demonstrate an apprehension of arrest based on specific allegations, establish that the prosecution is motivated by political, personal, or commercial malice, and physically present themselves before the High Court Division bench on the date of the hearing.

If the High Court Division finds prima facie evidence that a civil breach of contract has been deliberately criminalized to harass the petitioner, it typically grants anticipatory bail for a limited window (ranging from four to eight weeks) with a direction to surrender before the relevant Sessions Court. During this protected window, law enforcement agencies are prohibited from arresting the petitioner. For complete procedural protocols, consult our detailed resource on anticipatory bail under Section 498 CrPC.

sections.title: 6. Summary Matrix: Offence Elements, Bail Status & Statutory Penalties
sections.content:
The procedural distinctions between these interrelated sections dictate the defense strategy. The following table synthesizes the legal status of each provision under the Penal Code 1860 and CrPC 1898:

Penal Code Section Core Offence Allegation Police Power & Bail Status Maximum Statutory Penalty Trial Court Jurisdiction
Section 406 Criminal breach of trust Cognizable; Non-Bailable; Compoundable with court consent Imprisonment up to 3 years, or fine, or both Magistrate of the First Class
Section 420 Cheating & dishonest inducement to deliver property Cognizable; Bailable; Compoundable with court consent Imprisonment up to 7 years, and fine Magistrate of the First Class
Section 467 Forgery of valuable security, will, or trust document Cognizable; Non-Bailable; Non-Compoundable Imprisonment for life, or up to 10 years, and fine Court of Session / Special Magistrate
Section 468 Forgery committed for the purpose of cheating Cognizable; Non-Bailable; Non-Compoundable Imprisonment up to 7 years, and fine Magistrate of the First Class / Sessions
Section 471 Fraudulently using as genuine a forged document Cognizable; Bailable if forged doc bailable; Non-Compoundable Same punishment as for forging the document Court having jurisdiction over forged document

sections.title: 7. Quashing Malicious Criminal Proceedings under Section 561A CrPC
sections.content:
Securing bail provides temporary liberty, but the underlying criminal case remains pending for years unless dismissed or resolved. In situations where the dispute is overwhelmingly civil in nature—such as an alleged non-payment under a supply agreement, delay in land handover, or partnership accounting disagreement—the High Court Division possesses inherent jurisdiction under Section 561A of the CrPC to quash the proceedings.

To succeed in a quashing petition under Section 561A CrPC, the petitioner must demonstrate that the FIR or complaint, even if accepted on its face as true, does not disclose the essential legal elements of a criminal offence, or that the continuation of the trial constitutes a flagrant abuse of the process of the court. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has consistently established that a mere breach of contract does not give rise to criminal liability under Section 420 unless dishonest intent existed at the inception of the agreement.

Similarly, where Section 467 is alleged without producing the allegedly forged instrument or obtaining a handwriting examiner's forensic report, the High Court Division regularly issues a Rule Nisi accompanied by an order staying all further criminal proceedings in the subordinate court. To examine the grounds for terminating false criminal litigation, review our analysis on quashing criminal cases under Section 561A CrPC.

sections.title: 8. Illustrative Scenario: Managing a Weaponized Land Forgery Case
sections.content:
To illustrate how these interrelated provisions interact in practical litigation, consider the following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed).

A real estate developer in Gulshan entered into an agreement with a landowner to construct a multi-story residential complex. Due to delays in obtaining municipal building plan approvals from the development authority, project construction fell twelve months behind the original contractual schedule. Instead of filing a civil suit for breach of contract or seeking arbitration, the landowner lodged an FIR with the police station invoking Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, and 471 of the Penal Code.

The landowner alleged that the developer had dishonestly misappropriated advance funds (Section 406), fraudulently induced the contract (Section 420), and forged an addendum letter extending the construction timeline (Sections 467/468). Armed with the non-bailable Section 467 charge, police officers raided the developer's corporate offices. The developer immediately moved an anticipatory bail application before the High Court Division under Section 498 CrPC.

The High Court Division evaluated the primary contractual documents, observed that the dispute centered entirely on commercial performance and force majeure delays, and granted anticipatory bail for six weeks. Concurrently, the defense filed a Criminal Miscellaneous petition under Section 561A CrPC. The High Court issued a Rule Nisi and stayed all criminal proceedings, observing that converting a pure civil breach into a criminal forgery prosecution was an abuse of judicial process.

sections.title: 9. Essential Defense Checklist for Business Executives and Landowners
sections.content:
If you or your company are implicated in a criminal case involving Sections 406, 420, 467, 468, or 471, taking deliberate, structured steps will protect your liberty and preserve your legal defense:

  • Procure Certified Copies of the FIR / Complaint: Immediately obtain the formal ejahar or complaint copy from the court to identify the exact sections invoked and the specific factual assertions.
  • Secure Document Chains and Communications: Collect all written agreements, emails, bank transfer vouchers, and receipts demonstrating that money or property was transferred pursuant to a legitimate commercial transaction.
  • Do Not Evade Process Unrepresented: Evading police without an anticipatory bail petition risks proclamation and attachment under Sections 87 and 88 of the CrPC.
  • File for High Court Anticipatory Bail Immediately: If non-bailable sections (406, 467, 468) are present, approach the High Court Division under Section 498 CrPC before subordinate police arrest occurs.
  • Challenge Handwriting and Signatures Forensically: In forgery allegations, demand that questioned documents be forwarded to the Criminal Investigation Department (CID) forensic handwriting experts for scientific comparison.
  • Initiate Section 561A Quashing Proceedings: If the transaction is fundamentally contractual or governed by an arbitration clause, move the High Court Division to stay proceedings and terminate the frivolous prosecution.

faqs.question: Is Section 420 Penal Code bailable in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. Standalone Section 420 (cheating) is classified as a bailable offence under Schedule II of the Code of Criminal Procedure 1898. However, complainants rarely file Section 420 alone; they typically add non-bailable sections like 406 or 467.

faqs.question: Is Section 406 Penal Code bailable in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. Section 406 (criminal breach of trust) is classified as a non-bailable offence under Schedule II of the CrPC. Bail cannot be claimed as a matter of right and is subject to the judicial discretion of the court under Section 497 CrPC.

faqs.question: What is the punishment for forgery under Section 467 Penal Code?
faqs.answer: Section 467 carries severe penalties, including imprisonment for life, or rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, alongside a mandatory fine. Because of the potential life sentence, Magistrate Courts rarely grant bail.

faqs.question: Can Sections 406 and 420 be charged together in the same case?
faqs.answer: While complainants frequently bundle them, the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has repeatedly held that Sections 406 and 420 are conceptually inconsistent. Section 406 requires lawful entrustment followed by breach, whereas Section 420 requires fraudulent intention at the inception.

faqs.question: How can I obtain anticipatory bail if accused under Section 467?
faqs.answer: You must file an anticipatory bail application before the High Court Division under Section 498 of the CrPC. The applicant must appear in person before the bench and show that the charges are motivated by malice or arise from a civil commercial dispute.

faqs.question: What should I do if a business partner files a false 420 case against me?
faqs.answer: Secure all contracts, bank records, and correspondence proving that the matter is a civil breach of contract. Apply for bail, and subsequently petition the High Court Division under Section 561A CrPC to quash the criminal proceedings as an abuse of process.

faqs.question: Can an overseas Bangladeshi be arrested at Dhaka airport for a pending 420/406 warrant?
faqs.answer: Yes. If a Magistrate Court issues an arrest warrant and police notify immigration authorities, an overseas traveler can be offloaded and arrested upon arrival at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport unless anticipatory bail or a stay order has been secured.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Section 468 and Section 471 Penal Code?
faqs.answer: Section 468 punishes the actual act of forging a document with the intent to cheat. Section 471 punishes anyone who fraudulently uses an already forged document as genuine, knowing or having reason to believe it to be forged.
